title: What is known about 1RB0RE_1LC1LF_1RA1LD_0LB---_1RF1LE_0LB0RA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RE_1LC1LF_1RA1LD_0LB---_1RF1LE_0LB0RA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The tape is a list of blocks of the word 110, and a zigzag at each block boundary moves units from one block to the next. Each time the head returns to the left end, block i (counted from the left, i = 0, 1, 2, ...) has lost about 4i words, so the list acts like a base-4 counter. Lean proves the two shift rules of a sweep. The map on lists, with its carries and new blocks, has not been worked out.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 65,085 cells have been visited and 31,349 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 1.68×10<sup>19</sup> steps (exact macro run)
claims.text: A macro simulator (blocks of 6 cells, long runs of equal blocks crossed in one go; exact: every macro step is a run of the machine, counted step for step) ran from blank tape to step 16,848,971,644,337,937,408 without a halt. At this block size it gives the same state, head position and tape as the direct simulator after 2,000,004,826 steps. This is a bounded run and says nothing about later steps.

claims.title: Shift rules of a sweep
claims.text: sweep_left: going left, B turns n words 100 into 110 in 3n steps. sweep_right: going right, A and E turn n+1 words 110 back into 100 in 7n+9 steps. Both hold for every n and every surrounding tape.

claims.title: The exact law between refills
claims.text: Write the lists at visits to the left end with positions i = 0, 1, 2, ... Of the 13 pairs of consecutive visits up to step 1.86·10<sup>10</sup> whose lists parse as plain block lists, 10 follow one of two exact rules. In the first (5 pairs), block i loses exactly 4<sup>i</sup> words, and a new last block of 4<sup>r</sup>−1 words appears (15, 63, 1023, 4095, 16383). In the second (5 pairs), at the next visit that block has become 4<sup>r+1</sup>+3 (16387, 65539), and its left neighbour has lost 4<sup>r−1</sup>+1 instead of 4<sup>r−1</sup>. Example: [112,315,480,4642,15698,13634,8963,16383] at step 4,589,471,184 becomes [111,311,464,4578,15442,12610,4866,65539] at step 18,558,703,739.

claims.title: A base-4 counter
claims.text: Between two visits to the left end, block i loses about 4<sup>i</sup> words. A block that runs low is refilled, and new blocks appear at the right with lengths like 4095 = 4<sup>6</sup>−1 and 16387 = 4<sup>7</sup>+3. So the blocks behave like the digits of a base-4 counter that is counting down. The irregular part is what a refill does, since the refill amounts depend on the other blocks.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The machine halts if D reads a 1.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. The tape is a row of blocks, and the machine walks back and forth moving units from each block to the next. Seen from the left end, the blocks shrink by 1, 4, 16, 64, ... words: the row works like the digits of a base-4 counter.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 65,085 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: Blocks of 110
html: When the head is at the left end, the tape is 10 (110)^x0 1010 (110)^x1 1010 ... (110)^xr 10 11. On the way right, the blocks are rewritten as words 100; on the way left, they are turned back (sweep_right and sweep_left in Lean). At a boundary between two blocks the head zigzags. Each zigzag takes a little from the block on the left and adds one word to the block on the right.

From one row to the next, the blocks lose 1, 4, 16, 64, 256 and about 1024 words. This is a base-4 counter written in block lengths. The third block will soon run out (2 left), and what happens then, a refill whose size depends on the rest of the list, is the part not yet understood.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.47).
After 109 steps the tape spans 65,085 cells (49 left of the start, 50,841 right), with a density of 1s of 0.482.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: A list of blocks of 110 words: between visits of the head to the left end, block i shrinks by about 4^i, and blocks that run out are rebuilt; this behaves like a base-4 counter whose digits are block lengths.
family: base-4 counter on block lengths (block list)
